sections.body:
Altruism concerns readiness to help, contribute, and respond to others’ needs. It is not moral proof, unlimited self-sacrifice, people pleasing, impact assurance, or a requirement to abandon personal goals.

“Altruism within Agreeableness: readiness to help others” is used on this page as a descriptive construct within the NEO/IPIP-NEO 30-facet framework. The official IPIP resource describes scales that measure constructs similar to NEO facets and lists item mappings ([S11](https://ipip.ori.org/Finding_Scales_to_Measure_Particular_Constructs.htm)); this does not make scores from different instruments, translations, or products interchangeable.

FermatMind has not published product-level reliability, validity, Chinese norms, or individual predictive evidence for the score discussed on this page. This material is for self-observation and education. It is not for clinical diagnosis, hiring screening, school admission, or replacing a career decision.

> **Content method and update:** FermatMind Editorial prepared this page with AI-assisted drafting and checked terminology, boundaries, and evidence against public personality-psychology sources. It is for self-understanding and education; it is not clinical diagnosis, hiring screening, or individual-outcome prediction. Substantive update: 2026-07-19; review mode: solo_operator; not clinically reviewed.
sections.heading: Evidence and Interpretation Boundaries

sections.body: A stronger tendency notices opportunities to help and experiences helping as relatively natural. A weaker tendency may prioritize self-reliance, explicit reciprocity, or personal goals. Whether help is wanted, effective, sustainable, and fair remains a separate question.
sections.heading: Precise Definition

sections.body: Altruism belongs to [Agreeableness](/en/personality/big-five/agreeableness), reflecting interpersonal orientation toward assistance.
sections.heading: Parent Domain

sections.body:
- **Altruism versus Dutifulness:** Duty follows obligation; altruistic help may be voluntary.
- **Altruism versus people pleasing:** Approval seeking can motivate help, but is not required.
- **Altruism versus Tender-Mindedness:** [Tender-Mindedness](/en/personality/big-five/facets/tender-mindedness) concerns sympathetic concern; Altruism concerns readiness to act.
sections.heading: Distinguishing Neighboring Facets

sections.body: Stronger Altruism may appear as offering time, sharing resources, mentoring, or noticing workload. Weaker tendency may appear as waiting for a request, protecting capacity, or emphasizing reciprocal arrangements. Resources, caregiving burden, culture, and power shape visible helping.
sections.heading: Behavioral Cues

sections.body: Someone may help family extensively and avoid workplace favors, or contribute anonymously while declining emotional labor. Low capacity is not low care. A harmful request should not be honored merely to express a trait.
sections.heading: Contextual Differences

sections.body:
- Offering practical assistance without prompting.
- Sharing knowledge and access.
- Feeling satisfaction from contribution.
- Overcommitting or rescuing without consent.
- Neglecting personal needs and strategic priorities.
sections.heading: Possible Expressions When Stronger

sections.body:
- Asking for clear requests and roles.
- Protecting time and resources.
- Favoring reciprocal or system-level solutions.
- Missing unspoken needs.
- Contributing reliably when expectations are explicit.
sections.heading: Possible Expressions When Weaker

sections.body: Stronger Altruism can support mutual aid and cooperative capacity. Possible costs include exploitation, burnout, or ineffective help. Weaker Altruism can support boundaries and self-direction; possible costs include reduced support or relational friction. Neither level determines goodness.
sections.heading: Strengths and Costs

sections.body: A colleague offers one hour to teach a process, documents it, and declines to take over the whole project. Help increases capability without creating dependence.
sections.heading: An Original Case

sections.body: A person rarely volunteers spontaneously but funds a shared service and honors every explicit support commitment. Low spontaneous helping does not prove selfishness.
sections.heading: An Original Counterexample

sections.body:
1. Do you help before confirming what is wanted?
2. Which requests exceed current capacity?
3. Does help build capability or dependence?
4. What motive is present: care, duty, approval, guilt, or reciprocity?
5. Can you decline without treating yourself as bad?
sections.heading: Self-Observation Questions

sections.body: Choose one small requested help with a clear time boundary, or renegotiate one overextended commitment. Record effect on both people. The aim is useful, consensual help—not maximizing sacrifice.
sections.heading: Low-Risk Action Experiment

sections.body: Return to [Agreeableness](/en/personality/big-five/agreeableness) or the [30-facet guide](/en/personality/big-five/facets). Continue with [Trust](/en/personality/big-five/facets/trust), [Straightforwardness](/en/personality/big-five/facets/straightforwardness), [Compliance](/en/personality/big-five/facets/compliance), [Modesty](/en/personality/big-five/facets/modesty), [Tender-Mindedness](/en/personality/big-five/facets/tender-mindedness).
